title: Who Needs Cash Tonight

beats.text: In nineteen-oh-seven, a banker locked New York's bankers in his library and kept the key.
Imagine you're a young broker, buying stocks with money borrowed by the day.
Then a copper gamble blows up, and depositors stampede a trust company.
Nobody will lend. One-day money costs a hundred percent a year.
Lucky Lou dumps his best stocks at any price.
The exchange president begs Morgan: we have to close!
Morgan gives the banks ten minutes to find twenty-five million. They do.
So why would anyone sell good stocks so cheap?
You see, it's like needing rent by midnight. You'd sell your piano for twenty bucks.
Nine days later, Morgan locks the trust bosses in his library until they pledge twenty-five million.
In a panic, prices don't tell you what stocks are worth. Only who needs cash.

facts.claim: On the night of November 2-3, 1907, J. P. Morgan gathered bank and trust company heads in his library, locked the doors and kept the key in his pocket until the trust presidents agreed to a $25 million pledge; they signed in the early morning (about 4:45 a.m. / 'just after four' / conference broke up at five)
Stock-exchange houses financed positions with call loans (money lent day to day); on October 24, 1907 the call-money rate reached 100 percent (annualized)

The panic began when an attempt to corner United Copper stock failed (October 16, 1907), followed by a run on the Knickerbocker Trust Company, where depositors withdrew about $8 million before it suspended

On October 24, 1907, NYSE president Ransom H. Thomas told Morgan the exchange would have to close; Morgan told bank presidents $25 million must be raised in ten or twelve minutes; the subscription was filled by 2:16 p.m. and the floor roared/cheered
Morgan was seventy years old in 1907
The New York Stock Exchange fell almost 50% from its peak of the previous year (caption only)
The trust-company meeting was in Morgan's library; Morgan sat in the West Room, his office with red wallpaper and a fireplace, while bankers met in the East Room with three tiers of bookcases
The panic led to the founding of the Federal Reserve System in 1913 (caption only)
The young broker ('you') and his neighbour 'Lucky Lou' are fictional; the rent/piano line is an analogy

caption:
October 1907: overnight money on the New York Stock Exchange hit 100% interest. The exchange president wanted to close. J.P. Morgan, 70, gave the banks ten minutes to raise $25 million.
Nine days later he locked the trust bosses in his library until they signed. Stocks had fallen almost half from the year before.
